Transactions: from signed quote to revenue
Migrating from legacy CPQ to RLM

html:
Revenue Lifecycle Management (RLM) is the next-generation Revenue Cloud experience. Where classic CPQ ships as a managed package full of SBQQ__ objects, RLM is built directly on the Salesforce core object model: products, catalogs, selling models, price book entries, subscriptions, and transactions are all standard metadata that works with the declarative platform out of the box. This guide explains the modern RLM data model, how it replaces the legacy CPQ stack, and how subscription-centric quoting, ordering, and revenue flow through it. It is the foundation for everything that follows on automation (guide 12), analytics (guide 13), and certification (guide 14).

Learning objectives

  • Explain why Revenue Cloud introduced RLM and how it differs from the legacy SBQQ managed package.
  • Map the RLM object model: ProductCatalog, ProductCategory, ProductSellingModel, PriceBookEntry, and Subscription.
  • Model a product catalog with categories, specifications, and options.
  • Attach selling models and price book entries so a product can be quoted, sold, and renewed.
  • Describe how quotes become transactions and how subscriptions are created from a signed deal.
  • Model subscription relationships, amendments, usage, and renewal logic.
  • Compare the same business scenario implemented in legacy CPQ vs RLM objects.
  • Evaluate a data migration path from legacy CPQ to RLM.

RLM vs legacy CPQ: the two engines

Salesforce supports two engines for configure-price-quote and quote-to-cash:

DimensionLegacy CPQ (managed package)Revenue Lifecycle Management (RLM)
Delivery modelManaged package (SBQQ__ prefixed objects)Native core objects on standard metadata
Quote objectSBQQ__Quote__c, SBQQ__QuoteLine__cStandard Quote, QuoteLineItem (surfaced with CPQ behavior)
Price bookSBQQ__PriceBook__c + custom rulesStandard PriceBook / PriceBookEntry with ProductSellingModel
SubscriptionSBQQ__Subscription__cStandard Subscription object
OrderingOrder generated from quote linesTransaction / Order object from quote
ConfigurationSBQQ__ProductOption__c, SBQQ__ConfiguredAttribute__cProductSpecification, ProductOption with specification types
AutomationApex exposed by the packageFlows and Apex on core objects you fully own
Upgrade pathPackage version updatesSpring/Salesforce release upgrades, same as base platform
Tip: The certification exams test both engines. If you come from an org running SBQQ__Quote__c, RLM is a re-learn of the same concepts on different objects, not a re-learn of quoting itself.

The RLM data model map

Think of RLM as four layers:

text
1. CATALOG   ProductCatalog  ->  ProductCategory (tree)  ->  Product2
2. PRODUCT   Product2  +  ProductSpecification / ProductOption
3. PRICING   PriceBook / PriceBookEntry  +  ProductSellingModel  +  Prices/Matrices
4. TRANSACT  Quote  ->  Transaction (Order)  ->  Subscription  ->  Amendments

A product is useless for selling until it has a selling model (how it is sold) and a price book entry (what it costs). A subscription exists only after a transaction is fulfilled. Keeping these layers straight answers most RLM architecture questions.

Catalog Management: ProductCatalog and ProductCategory

The ProductCatalog object is the container that groups products for a sales organization. Every catalog has one or more category trees built from ProductCategory records.

  • A ProductCatalog represents a logical grouping (for example, "US Hardware Catalog" or "Global Cloud Services").
  • ProductCategory records form a self-referencing hierarchy called a category tree; each node can have children and belongs to exactly one catalog.
  • Products (Product2) are associated to categories through a categorized relationship, not by a lookup field on the product alone.

The canonical way to browse a catalog in SOQL:

soql
SELECT Name, (SELECT Product2Id, Product2.Name FROM ProductCategories)
FROM Product2
WHERE IsActive = true
LIMIT 50

On the catalog side:

soql
SELECT Id, Name,
       (SELECT Name FROM Categories)
FROM ProductCatalog
WHERE Name = 'Global Cloud Services'
Tip: Keep IsActive on Product2 accurate. Inactive products are filtered out of catalogs, selling models, and subscription product selection, which silently breaks flows that assume products still exist.

Products, specifications, and options

RLM describes what a product is with ProductSpecification and ProductSpecificationType, and how it can be configured with ProductOption and ProductOptionValue.

  • A specification groups related configuration attributes and can be Structural or Actional in type.
  • Options define discrete choices the customer makes (color, term, add-on module). Each ProductOption has values (ProductOptionValue) that can be required or mutually exclusive.
  • The configurable product links spec, options, and values together; the quote transaction stores the chosen option values so downstream fulfillment knows exactly what was sold.

A product with options conceptually maps to the legacy configurator:

text
Legacy SBQQ                                RLM
SBQQ__ProductOption__c            ->      ProductOption
SBQQ__ConfiguredAttribute__c      ->      ProductSpecification / ProductSpecificationType
SBQQ__OptionSelection__c          ->      Selected values on the quote record
Warning: Options affect pricing and ordering. A structural spec that is made actional later can change how the product is billed (for example, one-time vs recurring), so validate the specification type before you publish a catalog.

Selling models and price book entries

ProductSellingModel is the object that makes a product sellable. It describes how the product is sold: payment schedule, period, quantity rule, price method, and term. PriceBookEntry (core) holds the list price and its currency.

ConcernLegacy CPQRLM
Sell method / termSBQQ__Product__c pricing + subscription config fieldsProductSellingModel
List priceSBQQ__PriceBookEntry__c (custom)Standard PriceBookEntry
Volume / tier pricingSBQQ__PriceRule__cPrices and price matrices on entries
Discount behaviorDiscount schedules + SBQQ__DiscountSchedule__cPrice adjustments / price methods on the selling model

A selling model record is a child of the product + price book: it links ProductId, PriceBookEntryId, and the selling configuration. Keeping the selling model separate from the price book entry lets you sell the same product with different terms (monthly vs annual) and still share one list price.

apex
// Typical RLM query: product -> selling model -> price book entry
List<ProductSellingModel> models = [
    SELECT Id, Name, Product2Id, PriceBookEntryId,
           PriceBookEntry.UnitPrice,
           PriceBookEntry.PriceBook2.IsStandard
    FROM ProductSellingModel
    WHERE Product2Id = :productId
      AND IsActive = true
];

Quoting through RLM

Version 68 of the platform surfaces the classic Quote/QuoteLineItem objects with RLM behavior enabled. The quoting flow is close to legacy CPQ, but the configuration state and pricing come from the catalog objects instead of SBQQ__ records:

  1. A sales rep adds products to a quote; the price book entry and selling model drive the line.
  2. The configurator validates selected ProductOption values against the specification.
  3. Net pricing is calculated from list price minus discounts, using the same PriceRuleEngineService / QuoteCalculatorService shapes you already saw in the pricing module.
  4. The quote stores Approval_Status__c, Discount_Percent__c, Total_ARR__c, and other business fields used across the rest of quote-to-cash.
text
Product2 + ProductSellingModel + PriceBookEntry
                     |
                   Quote
                     |
                  QuoteLineItem(s)
                     |
              (close-won) -> Transaction -> Subscription(s)
Tip: Keep the CPQ standard custom fields you already depend on (Quote.ARR__c, QuoteLineItem.Net_Unit_Price__c, Quote.Uplift_Percent__c for renewals) consistent between the two engines. They are just fields; RLM fills them from selling-model pricing instead of price rules.

Subscriptions and amendments

The Subscription object is the heart of RLM. It represents revenue that repeats over time:

  • Fields include the subscribed product, PriceBookEntry snapshot, quantity, term, billing frequency, and Subscribe-State status.
  • Subscriptions cascade from a fulfilled quote transaction, or are created directly with Subscribe()-style operations from Apex/Flow.
  • Amendments capture changes to a subscription: quantity change, term extension, add-on product, or co-termination.
  • Usage-based components record consumption on the subscription and feed invoicing/billing.
  • Renewal logic mirrors what you built with Renewal_Opportunity__c and RenewalQuoteService: at renewal date, the subscription either renews (optionally with Uplift_Percent__c) or moves to a lost/renewal-risk bucket.
soql
SELECT Id, Name, SubscriptionNumber, Product2.Name,
       Quantity, Status, TermInDays,
       (SELECT Id, AmendmentNumber, EffectiveDate, Type FROM Amendments)
FROM Subscription
WHERE AccountId = :accountId
  AND Status = 'Active'
ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC
Tip: Distinguish sellable configuration (selling model) from committed state (subscription). A selling model controls the quote; the subscription is the contract-bound revenue record. Amending the quote does not amend the subscription until the change is accepted and committed.

Transactions: from signed quote to revenue

In RLM, an accepted quote produces a transaction (the RLM flavor of an Order). The transaction carries the money terms, and fulfillment turns it into assets/subscriptions:

  1. Quote is approved and closed-won.
  2. A transaction is generated with order management fields like Fulfillment_Status__c, Fulfillment_Date__c, and ERP_Order_Number__c.
  3. Fulfillment activates the subscription(s).
  4. Billing schedules (Revenue_Schedule__c) and revenue recognition begin.

The custom fields you built in the earlier modules plug straight in:

apex
Order theOrder = [SELECT Id, Fulfillment_Status__c, Fulfillment_Date__c,
                         ERP_Order_Number__c, Total_ARR__c
                  FROM Order WHERE Id = :orderId];
theOrder.Fulfillment_Status__c = 'Fulfilled';
theOrder.Fulfillment_Date__c = Date.today();
update theOrder;

Migrating from legacy CPQ to RLM

Moving a legacy org to RLM is a data and process migration, not just a field rename:

StepWhat changes
Inventory the packageFind every SBQQ__ object, field, and reference
Rebuild the catalogSBQQ__Product2 + config fields becomes ProductCatalog + ProductCategory + Product2
Recreate optionsSBQQ__ProductOption__c -> ProductSpecification + ProductOption
Recreate pricingSBQQ__PriceRule__c, discount schedules -> selling models + price book entries + prices
Rebuild automationsPackage-triggered Apex -> Trigger-handler services + Flows
Map subscriptionsSBQQ__Subscription__c -> standard Subscription, then replay amendments
Cut overRun both engines against staged data, compare quotes field by field
Warning: Do not treat RLM as "just a new API." Business rules that lived inside the package (validation, pricing, renewal calculations) now live in your org, so your flow/Apex coverage must be at least as good before you flip the switch.

RLM automation and integration hooks

Because RLM objects are core, everything from guide 12 applies directly: Trigger-handler services (QuoteTriggerHandlerService), platform events (Revenue_Sync__e) for quote-to-ERP sync, and HTTP callouts from PriceRuleEngineService work on Quote, QuoteLineItem, Subscription, and Transaction without package-specific wrappers. This is the single biggest operational advantage of RLM: the revenue objects are your metadata.

Hands-on walkthrough

This walkthrough mirrors exercises 11.1 (Compare CPQ vs RLM Objects) and 11.2 (Model a Subscription with RLM).

  1. In Setup, enable Revenue Cloud / RLM so the core objects (ProductCatalog, ProductSellingModel, Subscription, Transaction) are available in your API version 68.0 org.
  2. Create a ProductCatalog named "Cloud Services Catalog".
  3. Create a category tree: ProductCategory records for Infrastructure, Platform, and Applications nested under the catalog.
  4. Create three Product2 records (Compute, Storage, Support) and categorize each under the right ProductCategory.
  5. For Support, create a ProductSpecification with a ProductSpecificationType, then add a ProductOption for "Support tier" with values Silver / Gold / Platinum (one required value).
  6. Create a PriceBook (or use the standard one) and add PriceBookEntry rows for the three products with list prices.
  7. Attach a ProductSellingModel to each product that links Product2Id, PriceBookEntryId, price method, and term.
  8. Generate a Quote; add the three products as quote lines and exercise the Support option so the configuration saves with your chosen tier.
  9. Simulate an accepted deal: create the transaction and derive a Subscription for Support at term, then run the SOQL below to verify the model is coherent.
  10. Create an Amendment on the subscription increasing quantity by one, and compare the final SOQL output before and after.
soql
-- Verify the RLM model end to end
SELECT Id, Name,
       (SELECT Name FROM ProductCategories)
FROM Product2
WHERE Id IN (SELECT Product2Id FROM ProductSellingModel WHERE IsActive = true);

SELECT Id, Name, Product2.Name, Quantity, Status, TermInDays
FROM Subscription
WHERE PriceBookEntryId != null
ORDER BY SubscriptionNumber;

-- The legacy equivalent for the same deal (in a package org)
SELECT Id, SBQQ__Product__r.Name, SBQQ__Quantity__c, SBQQ__Status__c
FROM SBQQ__Subscription__c
WHERE SBQQ__Account__c = :accountId;

Compare the two SOQL results side by side: same business meaning, completely different objects. That is the CPQ-vs-RLM story in one query.

Common pitfalls

  • Treating RLM as a package. RLM is core metadata; there is no package to make your automations work.
  • Forgetting IsActive gates. An inactive product silently disappears from catalogs, selling models, and subscription creation.
  • Building product options without a specification type, so configuration never validates.
  • Pricing in the selling model while list price lives elsewhere, causing quote lines to disagree with the price book.
  • Editing selling models after quotes exist; historical quote behavior changes retroactively.
  • Using SBQQ__Subscription__c habits (custom status rollups) on the standard Subscription; write your own flows/trigger handlers.

Key takeaways

  • RLM is native Revenue Cloud: ProductCatalog, ProductCategory, ProductSellingModel, PriceBookEntry, Subscription, and Transaction instead of SBQQ__ objects.
  • Catalog stacks in layers: catalog -> category -> product -> specification/options -> selling model + price book entry -> quote -> transaction -> subscription.
  • Subscriptions are the revenue spine: amendments and usage update them between renewal cycles.
  • RLM's automation surface is ordinary Salesforce: triggers, flows, platform events, and callouts on core objects you own.
  • Know both engines for certification, but design new work on RLM objects to future-proof the org.
